new_statements.quote: Kru has both lexical and grammatical tone. Languages have either three or four register tones, which in this study will usually be marked in the following way: in a four-tone system, high tone will be marked by ˝, mid-high tone by ´, mid tone by ¯, and low tone by `. [...] What appear to be contour or modulated tones also occur in several languages. These are interpreted as a combination of two register tones [...] Tone plays an extremely important role in the grammatical systems of the Kru family, making such distinctions as perfective/imperfective aspect, possessive/relative/subject pronouns, definite/indefinite, and sometimes singular/plural.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere. The only opened description covering this language is a family-level overview: Kru languages (data includes Tchien Krahn = Eastern Krahn) have lexical and grammatical tone with three or four register tones; stress/accent is never mentioned. The Western-Krahn papers (Bing & Duitsman 1993 p. 92: 'The tonal systems of Krahn are complex and consist of rising and falling as well as level tones') likewise mention only tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source does not discuss stress at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level statement about Kru; Eastern Krahn is represented only through Tchien Krahn data (unpublished notes of Herb Tisher). Tone marks in the quote are scanned-reconstructed from the diacritic key; the passage was read from a scanned PDF with no text layer.
new_statements.identity_note: Eastern Krahn [kqo] = Glottolog east2414 'Konobo-Eastern Krahn'; Ethnologue dialects Gorbo, Kanneh, Konobo, Tchien (Chiehn). Marchese 1986 calls it 'Tchien Krahn' and groups it with Gbaeson Krahn under 'Western/Central Guéré (known as Krahn in Liberia)'. The opened Bing / Bing & Duitsman papers describe the Gbaeson and Gborbo dialects, which Glottolog assigns to Western Krahn [krw] (west2488), though SIL's own record 65116 codes the Bing & Duitsman ms as both kqo and krw. No source found describes Konobo, Kanneh or Gorbo phonology.

sources.note: §1.4.1 Phonology (pp. 12-16) is a family-level overview (syllable structure, consonants, vowel harmony, tone); p. 16 states Kru has lexical and grammatical tone with 3 or 4 register tones; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the front matter, data-base or phonology sections (PDF pp. 1-37 scanned). Tchien Krahn (= Eastern Krahn) data come from Herb Tisher's unpublished notes (p. 8).

Dialects Gorbo, Kanneh, Konobo, Tchien (Chiehn); NT 1996; no linguistic description.

sources.citation: Bing, Janet M. & John Duitsman. 1993. Postpositions and the valency marker in Krahn: monosemy versus polysemy. Journal of West African Languages 23(1): 91-104.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login: WID Old Widener 2235.3.35 (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Half-page phonological note p. 92: 'The tonal systems of Krahn are complex and consist of rising and falling as well as level tones' (tones numbered 1-4); fn. 3 refers to Duitsman 1978 for Gbaeson tone and Bing 1993 for Gborbo tone. Nothing on stress. Dialects treated are Gbaeson and Gborbo, which Glottolog assigns to Western Krahn [krw].
